blocks.text: Michaelis, in the Supplemm. vol. 4, p. 1080, on the authority of the Alexandrian and the Vulgate translators, interprets ילק as bruchus. He says that the bruchus is a little grub that creeps under the ground and ravages roots with its bite (in German Engerling), which afterwards becomes winged and is called by us Maykäfer, after the month of May. But for Jerome, Augustine and Remigius of Auxerre the bruchus is the young of the locust, as is clear from what Bochart cites below, p. 447 (marginal note). The Greek βροῦκος [broukos] or βρῦχος [brychos], moreover, signifies now the young of the locust, now a certain species of locusts. And at Ierem. LI, 27. the Alexandrian translators expressly put ἀκρίδα [akrida], the best-known name of the locust, for ילק. The Chaldee and the Syriac also understood a locust: the former renders it פרחא, winged locust, the latter ܣܡܐܢ ܠܐ ܦܪܚ, locust not yet winged. So far, then, is Bochart from assuming at his pleasure that ילק is a locust, as Michaelis asserts, that it is rather Michaelis himself who deserves censure, since he departed without reason from the authority of the ancients. Michaelis is refuted at length by Oedmann, Fasc. 2, Chapter 6, p. 126 ff., who himself takes ילק for the gryllus cristatus Linn. (Syst. Nat. vol. 1, part 4, p. 2074), common in those lands. He is moved chiefly by Ierem. LI, 27., where ילק is called סמר, which Oedmann interprets as serratus [serrated] and refers to the four-cleft keel of the thorax. But Tychsen, p. 91, renders the same סמר as horripilans [bristling], which he considers an epithet of the gryllus haematopus Linn. (p. 2075), with its hairy-fringed thighs. Bochart will give more on ילק סמר below, Chapter 2.

In the Talmudic tractate חלין Cholin, the סלעם is said to have a bald head, and the female to lack a sword-shaped tail. Since Tychsen finds these marks in the species of locust that Asso places third (and p. 5–6 of the German trans.) and calls gryllus eversor, he is persuaded, p. 69, that the Hebrew סלעם is that very species.

For Michaelis, in the Supplemm. p. 2094, צלצל is the same as חסיל, the gryllus with mole's feet, the gryllus talpiformis, to which he thinks the name was given from its shrill and sharp sound, following the authority of the Syriac translator, who puts ܨܪܨܘܪ, cricket. Against this opinion, however, not a few objections have been raised by Tychsen, p. 79–80, and by Oedmann, Fasc. 2, p. 140 ff., although he did not state his own opinion on צלצל. To Tychsen it seems an onomatopoeic name of the gryllus stridulus Linn. (vol. 1, part 4, p. 2078). The Alexandrians render it ἐρισυβην [erisybēn], which the Vulgate translator rendered rubigo [blight]. The same view was held by Jac. Hase in the Biblioth. Brem. Class 6, Fasc. 5, Diss. 1, § 9, who derives our word from צלה, he roasted, he scorched.

هذه الاسما كلها قد تكون الاصناف من الجراد [hādhihi al-asmā kulluhā qad takūn al-aṣnāf min al-jarād] all these names signify certain species of locusts, says R. Tanchum in his Commentary on Iocl I, 4., cited by Edw. Pococke on the same passage, p. 7.

From this also appears at once the emptiness both of the opinion of Andr. Norrelius (formerly librarian to the King of the Swedes), who, in his Diatriba de avibus esu licitis Levit. XI, 22., Uppsala 1746, contradicting all the ancients and following no usage of the oriental languages, makes ארבה doves, סלעם geese, חרגל the gallinaceous kind, and חגב sparrows, [III, 260] understanding the four on which they go of the four toes of the feet; and of that of J. D. Michaelis, who, in the Questions proposed to those about to travel to Arabia, p. 84 ff., and in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr., where he treats the individual names, thinks that not certain species of locusts but four stages of their life are designated, not considering that locusts cannot be eaten before they have begun to fly, to say nothing of the other objections raised against this opinion by Tychsen, p. 62 ff., and Oedmann, Fasc. 2, p. 88 ff., who also refuted Norrelius's fancies at greater length than was necessary.
Perhaps the Gryllus viridis of Forsskål (Descript. Animall. p. 81), with depressed, fringed thorax, spiny fore legs, and a yellow spot on each elytron. Common in the gardens at Alexandria.

To these add, from Niebuhr's Descript. Arab. p. 171, the red locust, Dsjerâd áchmar [جراد احمر] [jarād aḥmar], a migratory one, which, when it first arrives in the regions of Arabia, is small and lean, but after it has grown, to the great damage of the crops, is called Dsjerâd Mükken [جران مكن] [jarān mkn] [i.e. a locust laden with eggs], and is among the delicacies of the Arabs.

Among the people of Basra, جراد عصفور [jarād ʿuṣfūr] is the male of the Mukn مكن [mkn], the fertile egg-bearer, on the testimony of Niebuhr, p. 171. I shall quote his own words: At Basra the locust that the Arabs most like to eat was called Mukn. It was further added that this is the female, and very fat, or full of eggs, and that it is a strengthening food for men. Dsjerad asfur is the male of the Mukn, but lean, and is therefore not much used for eating at Basra.
